articles.headline: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip
keyFacts: Pope Leo XIV began a three-nation Latin America tour starting in Uruguay, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery.
The trip is the longest of the 71-year-old pope's pontificate and will also include visits to Argentina and Peru.
During his Uruguay visit, Pope Leo will meet President Yamandú Orsi and host Masses in multiple cities.
body: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip

ROME — Pope Leo XIV is kicking off a three-nation tour of Latin America with a visit to Uruguay, the region's least Catholic and most secular country, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.

Leo is due to arrive in Montevideo after a 13-and-a-half hour flight from Rome. He has a packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay including a visit to a neighborhood plagued by gang violence, a Mass in Paysandú, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, and another Mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometers (60 miles) away.

The Uruguay leg is the first stop on what will be the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate, all being undertaken as the 71-year-old pope continues his recovery. The trip will also bring him to neighboring Argentina and finally back home to Peru, where Leo served as a missionary priest and bishop for two decades.

"His stamina is fantastic. The way that he's singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong," said Maria Montserrat Alvar, the Vatican's new communications chief. She noted that Leo has passed the 14-day convalescence period required by doctors after his Oct. 13 surgery and is eager to get on the road.
"His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen, but we don't see that in his prognosis or even in the way that he's acting," she said.
A first stop in secular Uruguay

In Uruguay, which hasn't had a papal visit since 1988, Leo is expected to try to remind the 3.5 million people of their strong Catholic heritage stemming from the times of Spanish colonial rule. He is likely to propose the faith anew as an answer to today's challenges and problems.

Upon arrival, Leo will meet with President Yamandú Orsi, leader of the center-left alliance that assumed power in Uruguay in March 2025, and then deliver his welcome address to government officials and diplomats. He finishes the long day with a vespers service at the city's cathedral.

Leo will find in Uruguay a country unlike any other in Latin America, which is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics. Uruguay is considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people who identify as Catholic actually go to Mass regularly.

Uruguay was the first country in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use, the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion, and the third country in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage.

More recently, it became the first country in the region to approve assisted dying legislation over the strong opposition of the Catholic Church, evidence of Uruguay's entrenched, church-state separation that prohibits any mention of God in oaths of office.
Leo is expected to recall the church's opposition to abortion and euthanasia as part of his broader argument about upholding human dignity in all phases of life.

Uruguayan church officials have marveled at the apparent enthusiasm the visit has provoked, with reports that tickets to Leo's prayer vigil at Montevideo's Centenario Stadium were snapped up after two days.

"It seems that the pope's presence is shifting something here and is gradually breaking down this veil that has always sought to obscure and diminish the presence of the Catholic tradition that lies at the country's foundation," said Guzmán Carriquiry, the Uruguayan former head of the Vatican's pontifical commission for Latin America.
"I believe this pope will stir up questions in the hearts of Uruguayans -- disturbing questions -- questions about meaning and, we hope, questions about faith," he said.
Recalling the Catholic origins of independence
Carriquiry said he expects Leo will seek to revive the Catholic roots of Uruguay, especially when he travels to Florida on Sunday to mark an important Catholic feast day.

The Nov. 8 feast commemorates the Virgin of the Thirty-three, a small wooden icon of the Virgin Mary that is intricately connected to Uruguay's independence movement. According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in Florida on Aug. 25, 1825.

"So the number 33 is an ecclesiastical symbol, a national symbol," said Carriquiry, who was also Uruguay's ambassador to the Holy See. "And so the pope will speak there about the Catholic tradition that lies at the origin of Uruguay—that stems from Uruguay and gave rise to Uruguay—in order to revive and renew the Catholic tradition in the hearts of Uruguayans."

Andrew Chesnut, chair of Catholic studies and an expert in the Latin American church at Virginia Commonwealth University, said he wasn't surprised that Leo's visit had generated enthusiasm and that he will be welcomed warmly.

"But that's not necessarily going to translate into folks in the pews," he said. "If the overarching goal is trying to revitalize Catholicism in the most Catholic region on Earth, Uruguay is kind of a lost cause, and it has been for decades."

articles.headline: Global tech stocks tumble as blue wave is felt in Asia and Europe
keyFacts: Global tech stocks across Wall Street, Asia, and Europe dropped sharply following the U.S. midterm election results.
Success by anti-AI candidates raised fears that tighter Democratic scrutiny could delay AI infrastructure projects and increase costs.
J.P. Morgan strategist Tai Hui said Asian hardware demand should remain healthy over the medium term as computing demand grows.
body: HONG KONG — An intensifying rout of tech stocks hit global markets Friday, with a surge of red tickers spreading from Wall Street to Asia and Europe after the blue wave of the U.S. midterm elections fueled fears over AI development.

The steep losses in Asia — Japan’s Nikkei suffered its worst week since 2020 — came after a dramatic plunge in U.S. tech stocks following the success of anti-AI candidates, which deepened concerns about the durability of the AI boom.

Some $2.3 billion in market value was wiped off the tech-focused Nasdaq 100, which dropped 6.3% on Thursday. Another $2.8 trillion was erased from the S&P 500’s market value as it fell 4.4% — their worst day in 18 months, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets.
U.S. futures were mixed early Friday, but European shares also opened lower after the dramatic selloff continued in Asia.

South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 8%, triggering a temporary market-wide trading halt. There, AI data center memory suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in the early hours, before recovering some of their losses. Japan’s Nikkei 225 index fell as much as 6%, entering bear-market territory.
In Taiwan, home to some of the most critical AI companies, including chip supplier TSMC, the benchmark TAIEX index dropped 9%.
The picture was little better in Europe. London’s FTSE 100 index fell by nearly 2%, while the French and German indices, CAC40 and DAX, took similar hits.

“Markets are being punished according to their dependence on the U.S. AI infrastructure cycle,” Charu Chanana, Chief Investment Strategist at Singapore-based SAXO Markets, told NBC News in emailed comments.

The companies in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan are “clearly highly linked to the global AI capex cycle and hence I am not surprised to see the magnitude of correction today following the sharp correction in the U.S.,” Tai Hui, J.P. Morgan’s APAC Chief Market Strategist, told NBC News in emailed comments.

The plunge came after the stunning midterm results that will see a crop of anti-AI and anti-data center politicians take office, including Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, the largest data center market in the country.

The Democratic Congress could tighten scrutiny of the industry, including AI infrastructure projects, which could cause delays and additional costs, adding to worries investors have about the profitability of these investments.
Asian markets were already in trouble

The months leading up to the American election had already been a rollercoaster for Asian investors, who saw their fortunes soar in June during the AI stock boom, but have been suffering from a brutal recent sell-off.
A sense that initial valuations of key AI companies were inflated was troublesome enough for markets in Asia, but the Democratic sweep has introduced another layer of uncertainty.
Markets had largely expected losses for Trump’s Republicans, but not on this scale.
“This matters enormously for Asia because much of the hardware supporting America’s AI ambitions is manufactured here,” Chanana, from SAXO Markets, said.
Some of the Asian companies at the heart of the AI supply chain surged to astonishing heights.
The Chinese market offered access to frontier AI companies that recently began going public — months earlier than their American counterparts like Anthropic, which is still preparing for its IPO.
Model maker Z.ai rose by 2,000% in June after debuting in January.
But corrections came swiftly, with Z.ai now down over 80% since its peak and on Friday shedding another 10%.

Lofty valuations of other Chinese companies have also cratered, with mainland China’s Star 50 index, which comprises the country’s semiconductor and AI leaders, now at half of its June peak with half a trillion in market value wiped out.
On Friday, both the tech-focused Star 50 and the AI Index slumped as much as 5% before recouping some losses.
“There is a legitimate argument that parts of China’s AI equity bubble have already burst,” Chanana said.
But she added that unlike the U.S., where much of the investment is commercially driven, “China treats AI and semiconductor self-sufficiency as strategic national priorities.”
“This means investment can continue for reasons beyond immediate profitability, including technological independence, industrial competitiveness and national security.”

That is not the case in South Korea, whose market darlings, memory makers SK Hynix and Samsung, are an integral part of the commercial AI buildout. That makes the country particularly sensitive to any U.S. slowdowns.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index more than doubled in market value in June, but by Friday had shed most of the gains made this year. Like South Korea, there is acute exposure for Taiwan — key for advanced chip manufacturing and TSMC’s headquarters.
Nevertheless, most of the Asian indexes are still higher than they were a year ago: South Korea’s Kospi is up 25%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 is up 13%, and TSEC Taiwan Technology is also up by 47%.

“For semiconductor and memory makers in Asia Pacific, as long as global demand for computing power continues to grow, demand for the underlying hardware should remain healthy over the medium term,” J.P. Morgan’s Hui said.
“There may be constraints on where the ‘gold’ can be mined, but as long as demand for the gold remains, the picks and shovels will still be needed elsewhere,” he added.

articles.headline: Rosie O’Donnell considers return to New York from Dublin after celebrating blue wave of midterm election wins
keyFacts: Rosie O’Donnell told The Washington Post she is considering returning to New York from Dublin following midterm election results.
O’Donnell stated she wants to return because she misses her grown children and her six-month-old grandson.
The White House responded in a statement calling O’Donnell a nasty woman whose brain was completely destroyed by Trump Derangement Syndrome.
body: Rosie O’Donnell considers return to New York from Dublin after celebrating blue wave of midterm election wins
By
Tracy Wright, Fox News
Published Nov. 6, 2026, 2:36 a.m. ET
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Rosie O’Donnell dabbled in the idea of returning to the States while celebrating the midterm election results.
O’Donnell – a consistent critic of the current administration – fled the United States for Ireland after Donald Trump was elected president for a second term in 2024.

While the former talk show host relished life across the pond, she’s now thinking about moving back home to New York, and told The Washington Post that Dublin is “beautiful — we love it here, but my family’s not here.”
She added, “And I miss my grown kids. I miss my grandson that was born six months ago. And I feel like I’ve missed half his life already and don’t want to miss any more.”
The “A League of Their Own” star has four children with ex-wife Kelli Carpenter, and one child with late ex-wife Michelle Rounds.
“It’s a beautiful morning in the world,” she said. “The Trump regime is over, thank you America. I knew we would do it; I knew it in my heart.”
“You gotta believe people, and you did, and you showed up. And we gave a very loud and clear message to Trump … and his partners in cruelty. His criminal friends – Enough, we’ve had enough.”
O’Donnell noted that she “went to bed early” in Dublin while returns came back on election night in the States.
“I didn’t think I could stay up; I was so anxious,” she said. “I went to bed and at 3 o’clock in the morning – ding, ding, ding, ding – everyone started texting me and I started to cry.”
“I was so overwhelmed with emotion – overwhelmed – and I got up this morning and I took a shower and I put on my blue jumper … and I’m like, I’m wearing blue today.”

O’Donnell said she was “so proud of all of us, of our country” before reflecting on the “unconstitutional, un-American things that this administration has perpetrated on the people of this country and the world.”
“Let the investigations begin, really,” O’Donnell said. “This is a glorious day.”
The White House responded in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying, “Rosie O’Donnell is a nasty woman and a total slob whose brain has been completely destroyed by Trump Derangement Syndrome.”
“I’ve really enjoyed my time here thanks to everyone who’s been watching this week, especially the hungry, hungry hypocrite in the White House,” she said during her final opening monologue.
“Most of all, I’d like to thank Jimmy Kimmel for inviting me to do this and for reminding everyone that we have the right to free speech in this country, whether orange Voldemort likes it or not.”
O’Donnell and the president have traded jabs for years, and Trump threatened to revoke the comedian’s citizenship after she fled to Ireland in 2025.

The decades-long feud stems back to 2006 after O’Donnell criticized him when she was a host on “The View” about his decision to be lenient toward a Miss USA winner who had been accused of drug use and other bad behavior.

articles.headline: After Buying EA, Silver Lake and PIF Are Reportedly Now Seeking to Acquire Gaming Software Provider Unity
keyFacts: A consortium including Silver Lake and the PIF recently held talks to acquire gaming software provider Unity, according to a Reuters report citing confidential sources.
Unity has consulted with an investment bank to evaluate options, though the talks remain preliminary and no deal is guaranteed, sources stated.
Following news of the acquisition talks, Unity shares rose nearly 15% in regular trading to reach $48.80 per share.
body: A consortium of investors including private equity firm Silver Lake Partners and Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund PIF has held recent talks to acquire gaming software provider Unity.

A Reuters report citing confidential sources familiar with the matter states that PIF and Silver Lake, the latter of which already owns 8% of Unity, approached the company in recent weeks. The buyer consortium discussed a valuation of about $25 billion before Unity’s latest earnings report, which lifted its market capitalization to roughly $21.5 billion.
Unity has reportedly been consulting with an investment bank to evaluate its options following the approach, however talks are preliminary and no deal is assured.

Should the acquisition go ahead, this would be another major investment into the games industry for Silver Lake and PIF. The two firms previously teamed up with Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners to acquire Electronic Arts for $55 billion in a deal that was finalised in August . Since then the publisher has initiated major corporate restructurings and studio closures, most recently shutting development studio BioWare and cancelling the next Mass Effect game .

Unity’s popular game engine and development tools have been used to create thousands of mobile, console, and PC games. These include Genshin Impact, Hollow Knight, Among Us, Subnautica, and Beat Saber, to name just a few. Notably, Unity’s tools are also used by Scopely, the developer of Monopoly Go!, and Niantic, the maker of Pokemon Go, both of which are owned by a group that includes Silver Lake, PIF, and Affinity Partners.

Silver Lake has already invested $400 million into Unity and with its 8% stake it remains one of its largest shareholders. Since going public in 2020, Unity has expanded beyond its game engine business into advertising technology and broader real-time 3D software, and its tools are increasingly used in automotive design, filmmaking, architecture, and industrial simulation.
After news of the acquisition talks first broke, Unity shares rose nearly 15% in regular trading and sit at $48.80 per share at the time of writing.

articles.headline: Blue Origin says it is building a higher-performing rocket engine at 1/4 the cost
keyFacts: Blue Origin announced upgrades to its New Glenn rocket, including a new engine and a third stage to expand payload capacity and reduce manufacturing costs, CEO Dave Limp said.
The company is developing the Northstar engine to eventually replace the BE-4, featuring higher thrust, fewer parts, and a production cost that is 25 percent of the BE-4, according to Limp.
Blue Origin has already begun test-firing the Northstar engine and continues to manufacture the BE-4 for United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket.
body: KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Fla.—Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon.
With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.
“There has never been higher demand for launch, ever,” Dave Limp, chief executive officer of Blue Origin, said during the UP.Summit conference at the Shuttle Landing Facility in Florida.

Blue Origin has already begun test firing a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. Separately, the company also said it was developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket, GS3, to give it an extra kick.
A new Northstar
The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine, Limp said. It has half the number of parts, 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed.

Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent of the cost of a BE-4 engine, and eventually reach the point where each engine can be assembled in less than a day. The company is deep into development and testing of Northstar, having already begun a test-firing campaign.
“To get access to space at a lower cost, we have to look at every part of the vehicle,” Limp said. “This is going to be a game-changer.”

The BE-4 engine powering New Glenn today has a thrust of 640,000 pounds, and Limp said Northstar will have a starting thrust of 715,000 pounds. Like the BE-4 engine, Northstar burns methane and liquid oxygen using an oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle and a single-shaft turbopump architecture.
Limp said the company will continue to manufacture the existing BE-4 engine for United Launch Alliance, which uses two of the engines to power its Vulcan rocket.

articles.headline: What the midterms could mean for Trump’s Cabinet
keyFacts: President Donald Trump's administration faces potential Cabinet shakeups following recent midterm election losses before Democrats take control of Congress.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth are among the officials who could potentially leave the administration.
Trump likely needs to get Cabinet replacements confirmed during the final two months of the current Republican Senate majority.
body: President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at a news conference during the NATO Summit in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026. | Krisztian Bocsi/Bloomberg via Getty Images
This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .
Welcome to The Logoff: It’s a whole new world for President Donald Trump.

What’s happening? So far, surprisingly little: As we wrote yesterday, Trump has largely stayed quiet since his shellacking in Tuesday’s midterms ( ballroom tour aside), and that continued on Thursday.
With the days counting down until Democrats take control of Congress, though, there are signs that things could begin to shift in his administration.

What could happen? A Cabinet shakeup, whether that means firings, resignations, or something in between. It’s not unusual after any midterm, and especially not after a loss this seismic (Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld stepped down the day after the 2006 midterms amid voter anger about Iraq).

Whatever happens, though, might need to happen fairly soon: It’s always possible that Trump could skate by with acting secretaries (he’s previously said he’s a fan ), but if he wants to get replacements confirmed, he’ll likely need to do it in the final two months of the current Republican Senate majority.
Who’s eyeing the exits? Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , potentially — but for very different reasons.

In Rubio’s case, it would give him a chance to distance himself from a radioactively unpopular presidency ahead of a potential 2028 presidential run — particularly as Vice President JD Vance is stuck writing social media posts about why the Iran war was maybe a bad idea .

Hegseth, meanwhile, is one of the public faces of the war. Trump has — for now — denied any designs on replacing Hegseth, but the secretary faces the prospect of impeachment as soon as next week. He’s also reportedly interested in being appointed to a soon-to-be-vacant US Senate seat for Tennessee, which would provide him a convenient escape (though based on Tuesday’s results , he might be an underdog to win an election anywhere in America).

What’s the big picture? We don’t yet know anything for sure about what’s next, but the chatter is reflective of the new world Trump and his administration are facing: dismally unpopular, deprived of easy confirmation hearings and cover from Republicans in Congress, and facing an aggressive oversight agenda.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

articles.headline: Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
keyFacts: SpaceX and Tesla shares dropped significantly as tech and AI stocks plummeted following the Democratic victory in the US midterm elections.
Investors are concerned about potential tougher scrutiny of data center construction and fears that AI infrastructure investments may not deliver expected returns.
Tech leaders including OpenAI's Greg Brockman acknowledged the need to improve communication regarding the benefits of AI and data centers to local communities.
body: - Published
Shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX have plunged as tech and artificial intelligence stocks more broadly plummeted a day after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterms.
Those losses dragged the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index down, which had fallen by more than 5% at one point in early trading.
The market has been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the artificial intelligence (AI) industry following Democrat wins in key data centre states including Texas.
Following the election, some tech leaders have acknowledged they need to improve their communication around data centres and the benefits of AI.
SpaceX shares were down more than 9% in by lunchtime in Thursday trading, while Tesla shares dropped more than 11%.

Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Shares in chipmakers have been suffering, with AMD dropping more than 14% on Thursday, while Micron shares had dropped by as much as 17% before recovering slightly.
Intel shares are down by more than 7% and shares in Nvidia have fallen nearly 9%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had fallen by 10%.
The stock falls also hit the S&P 500 index, which dropped by 3.8% by lunchtime.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.

"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.

"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick agreed that the industry needed to improve their communication about the benefits of AI.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction.
